name: Noone
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Hyman, Larry M. (1981). Noni Grammatical Structure, with Special Reference to Verb Morphology. SCOPIL 9, USC. Cited in Wikipedia Noone article; no online copy located.

new_statements.quote: 1. Each syllable carries contrastive tone in Noni. Three level (register) tones characterize the language: H (high), M (mid) and L (low). These three levels are represented by means of the three accent marks á, ā and à, as seen in the following examples: [...] The language also makes use of a number of contour tones involving a change from one of the three tone levels to another within the same syllable. Of the six logical possibilities (LH, LM, MH, HL, MH, ML), only MH does not exist in the language. [...] In all cases the domain of tone is the syllable.
new_statements.citation: Hyman, Larry M. 1981. Noni Grammatical Structure, with Special Reference to Verb Morphology. Southern California Occasional Papers in Linguistics (SCOPIL) 9. Los Angeles: Department of Linguistics, University of Southern California. vi+121 pp.
new_statements.locator: Part I: Phonology, Chapter 2 'The Tone System', section 1, printed p. 5 (pdf page 11 of the scan); Chapter 1 'The Sound System' printed pp. 1-4 (pdf pp. 7-10) likewise contains no mention of stress
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given. The only accessible primary description (Hyman 1981) treats Noni as a three-level register tone language (H, M, L plus LH, LM, HL, HM, ML contours, and a rare LHL) with the syllable as the tone-bearing unit; a grep of the scanned of all 127 scanned pages for stress/accent/prominence/intensity finds no phonological statement about stress (the word 'accent' occurs only as 'accent marks' for tone; 'prominence' on printed pp. 105-106 is syntactic focus). Hyman also notes there is no downdrift (Ch. 2 section 2, p. 6).
new_statements.exceptions: None relevant; tonal notes only (LH realized LM before H/L/pause; M optionally lowered between L_H and H_L; nouns keep isolation tones in context, verbs alternate tonally by tense/aspect).
new_statements.domain_note: This is a tone statement, not a stress statement: the source is silent on stress. Domain of tone = the syllable; nouns cited in isolation (citation forms) and in phrase context.
new_statements.identity_note: Hyman 1981 describes 'Noni' as spoken at Nkor (consultant Mark Bintum of Nkor); this is the language-level noon1243 (Glottolog alternate names Noni, Nooni, Kumaju), no dialect issue. The only other open Beboid description fetched sources, Boutwell 2020, is a grammar of Nchane (ncha1245), a different Beboid language, and was used only for context and bibliography.

sources.note: Nothing. Part I (Ch.1 Sound System pp.1-4, Ch.2 Tone System pp.5-6) describes seven short/long vowels, consonants, syllable structure (N)C1(G)V1(V2)(C2), and a three-level tone system with contours, 'Each syllable carries contrastive tone in Noni' (p.5); scanned of all 127 pdf pages has no stress/accent/prominence statement (image-only scan, scanned at 200 dpi).
Nothing on phonology; bibliography lists Hyman 1980, Hyman 1981, Lux 2003 Noni Provisional Lexicon (ms., SIL Yaoundé), Richards 1991, Boutwell 2020.

sources.citation: Boutwell, Richard L. 2020. A Grammar of Nchane: A Bantoid (Beboid) Language of Cameroon. LOT 572. Leiden University PhD dissertation.
sources.note: DIFFERENT LANGUAGE (Nchane, ncha1245). For Nchane only: vowel laxing 'is less likely to occur if the vowel is in a position associated with stress (as indicated by an apparent increase in intensity), such as root initial... Note that stress as a feature of the sound system has not been studied beyond the observances made here' (Ch. Phonology, pp. 39-40). Says nothing about stress in Noni; cites Hyman 1981, Richards 1991, Andrus & Lux 2009, Lux 2016 for Noni.
Segment inventory only (UPSID 492, presumably from Hyman 1981); no stress or tone information.
